title: Jevil: A Catastrophic-Failure-by-Design Signature Scheme
abstract:
Few-time signatures cap how many signatures a signer can safely issue. Jevil is, to our knowledge, the first post-quantum and transparent (setup-free) few-time signature scheme with a sharp key-recovery cliff: its cap is enforced by a single sharp threshold rather than a slow slope. Signatures one through $n^{\star}$ are existentially unforgeable at approximately $124$-bit classical security; at the $(n^{\star}{+}1)$-th the entire secret polynomial becomes publicly recoverable, achieving catastrophic failure as a key design requirement. The cap is founded on a secret polynomial together with the degree-binding of a polynomial commitment, and is intrinsic to any accepted public key: even a malicious signer who chooses $\mathsf{pk}$ adversarially cannot construct one that lets them keep signing past the cliff without the same polynomial becoming publicly recoverable.

All prior post-quantum few-time schemes (HORS, FORS, PORS, HORSIC$^{+}$, eBiBa, Syrga$_2$) degrade softly as $(nK/T)^K$. Every prior cliff-style construction misses at least one of post-quantum, transparent, sharp, and count-triggered: one-time Schnorr/ECDSA nonce reuse is neither post-quantum nor a designed property; polynomial-witness key-extraction signatures (notably DSKE) over KZG or IPA commitments are sharp but neither post-quantum nor transparent, while DSKE's hash-based variant is post-quantum and transparent but degrades softly; and double-authentication-preventing signatures (DAPS), post-quantum and transparent in their lattice form, fire a sharp key-recovery cliff on a message predicate (signing conflicting messages) rather than on a signature count, so they are not few-time schemes.

Concretely, Jevil provides $68$-byte public keys, $32$-byte secret keys, and $\sim 40$~KB to $\sim 500$~KB signatures across the recommended signing budgets $n^{\star} \in \{1, 3, 7, 15, \ldots, 2^{14} - 1\}$, the range admitted by the working field's $2$-adicity. All primitives are believed to be post-quantum.

1      Introduction
A few-time signature (FTS) scheme caps how many signatures a signer can safely issue.

In their bare form, FTSs are just a simple numbers game: interesting in their own right
whenever an application has intrinsic finitude (a firmware vendor capping their own release
count, an operator binding themselves to a per-tenure attestation budget, an ephemeral
session signer, any audit-budgeted credential that issues its allowance and then would just
as soon sleep for the other 100 years), and one wants a cryptographic guarantee on that
cap, not a policy promise.
    The natural way to enforce a count cap is statefully: a counter, a synced database, a
hardware register. Stateful schemes are notoriously fragile in deployment: a single counter
rollback (a restored backup, a cloned VM, a forked container) silently re-uses key material
and breaks security. Stateless schemes route around this by making the cap a property
of the cryptographic object itself rather than the signer’s discipline. HORS is stateless in
this sense, but its degradation is soft: at n signatures, forgery probability rises gradually
as (nK/T )K , so “how many signatures is safe” is a slider on a continuum.
    This paper presents Jevil, a self-enforcing FTS whose degradation is the opposite of
soft. The signer picks a budget n⋆ at KeyGen from the set {1, 3, 7, 15, . . . , 214 − 1} (the
values for which (n⋆ +1)K is exactly a power of two). Signatures 1, . . . , n⋆ are existentially
unforgeable at approximately 124-bit classical security against adversaries making at most
2128 random-oracle queries (Theorem 4). At the (n⋆ +1)-th signature the entire secret
polynomial becomes publicly recoverable in O(D2 ) field operations. The cap is enforced
not by a counter but by the algebraic structure of a single secret polynomial together
with the degree-binding of a polynomial commitment. Crucially, the cliff is intrinsic to
any accepted public key, not a property of honest KeyGen: a malicious signer who chooses
pk adversarially in the hope of signing indefinitely cannot escape it (Corollary 2). To the
best of our knowledge, Jevil is the first post-quantum, transparent (setup-free) few-time
signature scheme whose key-recovery threshold is sharp rather than soft (§2).

2     Related work
We organise prior work along two axes that together pick out the design point Jevil occu-
pies: degradation shape (soft slope vs. sharp cliff) and assumption profile (post-quantum
and transparent vs. classical or setup-dependent). Table 1 summarises the resulting land-
scape; the remainder of this section walks through each family.

HORS-family few-time signatures (soft degradation). The dominant FTS family
descends from BiBa [1] and its successor HORS [2], both built on t-subset-resilient func-
tions: a secret key is a list of T pre-images, and a signature publishes the K pre-images
at message-derived positions. After n signatures, an adversary’s forgery succeeds with
probability at most (nK/T )K by the standard coverage bound; this is a soft curve that
approaches but never reaches certainty. PORS [3] and HORST tighten the constants by
using pseudo-random subsets and Merkle authentication respectively, but preserve the
soft-degradation profile. FORS, the FTS at the leaves of SPHINCS+ [4] and the stan-
dardised SLH-DSA [5], replaces HORS with a forest of authenticated trees; the leaf-level
degradation is still the same coverage curve. More recent variants such as HORSIC+ [13],
eBiBa [14], and Syrga2 [15] continue this lineage with size or speed improvements but un-
changed degradation shape. In every case, the operationally meaningful cap is the largest
n for which the coverage bound stays below a chosen probability; there is no n⋆ after
which the key becomes recoverable in any meaningful sense.

Stateful hash-based signatures. XMSS, LMS, and the stateful variants of SLH-DSA
cap signatures with a counter. Over-signing is prevented, not punished: the signer simply
refuses to issue past the budget. The cap is hard in the sense that the signer can’t go past
it without falsifying state, but it is enforced by signer discipline plus durable storage, not
by anything algebraic. The well-known failure mode: counter rollback (restored backup,
cloned VM, forked container) re-uses state and silently breaks security. That fragility is
what motivated the stateless SPHINCS+ /SLH-DSA line in the first place.

Cliff-style behaviour from nonce reuse. Standard Schnorr and ECDSA signatures
exhibit a different kind of cliff: any two signatures produced with the same nonce k permit
linear key recovery from σ1 − σ2 = k −1 (h1 − h2 ). This is the closest geometric analogue
to Jevil’s cliff (one extra signature ⇒ full key recovery). However: (i) the cliff is at n = 2
(the schemes are one-time under nonce reuse, not few-time); (ii) it is an unintended failure
mode of the implementation, not a designed property of the scheme; (iii) Schnorr and
ECDSA rest on the discrete-log assumption and are not post-quantum. We list nonce
reuse here only because it is the most often-cited example of “n + 1 signatures reveal the
key,” to make clear that Jevil’s cliff is qualitatively different: a designed, configurable
threshold at n⋆ + 1 within a post-quantum FTS.

Cliff-style behaviour from double-spending. Chaum-style offline electronic
cash [16, 17] embeds a designed cliff: a user who spends the same coin twice has her
identity (not her signing key) cryptographically extracted by the bank. Subsequent
refinements [18] extend this to fair e-cash schemes with opening authorities. The
geometry is similar (one extra use opens what one use kept hidden), but the setting
is different: an interactive bank-merchant-user protocol, not a stand-alone signature
scheme, with the recovered object being the user’s identity inside a group-signature-like
construction rather than the secret signing key. None of the well-known constructions in
this line are believed to be post-quantum.

Self-enforcement: DAPS and PAPS. Double-authentication-preventing signatures
(DAPS) [26, 27] embed a designed key-recovery cliff of a different flavour: a signer who ever
signs two messages sharing a subject but differing in payload thereby exposes their own
signing key. Boneh, Kim, and Nikolaenko [28] give the first lattice-based DAPS (hence
the first post-quantum, transparent one) and generalise it to predicate-authentication-
preventing signatures (PAPS), where signing any tuple of messages satisfying a fixed
predicate ϕ leaks the key. On the assumption axis this is the closest prior work to Jevil:
the cliff is sharp (one offending tuple recovers the key in full), and the lattice instance is

Polynomial-witness FTSs. A line of work commits to a degree-D polynomial and
signs by opening K evaluations; the Lagrange-interpolation cliff at ⌈(D + 1)/K⌉ is then
intrinsic to the scheme. Figure 1 illustrates the cliff geometry at toy parameters K = 2,
n⋆ = 1. Constructions in this family typically use KZG [19]5 or inner-product argument

a trusted setup (KZG) or a discrete-log assumption (KZG and IPA both). These schemes
thus share Jevil’s cliff geometry, but none are simultaneously post-quantum and transpar-

from FRI [22], DEEP-FRI [9], and STIR [8]);7 this brings the cliff into the post-quantum
and transparent setting without losing the sharp threshold.

Threshold and secret-sharing-based signatures. Shamir [23]8 and Pedersen [24]9
secret sharing encode a secret as a degree-D polynomial recoverable from D + 1 evalu-
ations; threshold signatures (BLS threshold, threshold Schnorr/ECDSA)10 exploit this.
Jevil rests on the same Lagrange-interpolation fact but inverts its role: where threshold
cryptography distributes evaluations across parties at KeyGen as the intended reconstruc-
tion path, Jevil accumulates them across a single signer’s openings as the penalty for
over-use, with evaluation positions tied to message hashes rather than party identities.

Hash-based polynomial commitments. zk-WHIR [7] is an honest-verifier zero-
knowledge variant of WHIR, itself the most recent in a line of Reed–Solomon proximity
tests (FRI [22], DEEP-FRI [9], STIR [8]) used as polynomial commitments in succinct
arguments. We use zk-WHIR for its fast verifier, its linear-form opening interface, and
its honest-verifier zero-knowledge guarantee; all three fit the lift cleanly.

8     Discussion
Comparison with stateful HBS. Stateful schemes (XMSS, LMS)53 cap signatures
with a counter, and state-sync failures are silently catastrophic: a rolled-back counter
re-uses key material and breaks unforgeability with no outward sign. Jevil also asks the
signer to stop at n⋆ (that discipline does not disappear), but it relocates the consequence
of failing to do so into the cryptographic object: a Jevil signer who oversigns publishes the
polynomial. The difference is accountability, not the absence of a cap to respect. Where
a stateful over-sign fails silently and in the signer’s favour (they keep producing accepting
signatures), a Jevil over-sign fails loudly and against the signer (the key becomes public),
so over-use is detectable by any observer and cannot be undone by restoring a backup.

Comparison with HORS-family schemes. HORS gets a stateless cap from t-subset
coverage; security degrades gradually as (nK/T )K . Jevil keeps the HORS coverage anal-
ysis intact below the cap and bolts a polynomial-recovery cliff on top. The cliff makes
over-signing visibly disastrous: if the signer oversigns, the world reconstructs the polyno-
mial in O(D2 ), and there is no damage control left to do.
